crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Explaining research after publication covers the work of turning a published paper into accessible summaries, annotations, and discussions for readers beyond the original authors. It includes plain language summaries, graphical abstracts, video explainers, and post-publication peer review. The goal is to make findings, methods, and limitations understandable without requiring specialist training. This work sits between the formal record and public or interdisciplinary audiences.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on the published paper itself, supplementary materials, and any registered data or code. Practitioners use reference managers, annotation platforms, and document editing tools to track claims and sources. Some groups maintain internal libraries of papers and extracted claims, such as the 135 research papers and 11,075 claims held on this site, to support consistent explanations. No special hardware is required beyond standard office and web tools.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The typical method starts with close reading of the abstract, methods, results, and limitations. The explainer identifies the research question, the main claim, the evidence, and the uncertainty around it. They then rewrite the content in plain language, often using short sentences and concrete examples, while preserving the original meaning. Peer reviewers or editors check the explanation against the paper to catch drift or overstatement.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk center on accuracy, attribution, and consent. Explainers must not alter the scientific meaning or imply endorsement by the original authors. They should link to the original paper rather than to secondary search tools, as this site does, so readers can verify the source. Misrepresentation, selective quoting, or removing caveats can create legal and reputational risk for both the explainer and the platform. Provenance matters: every summary should make clear which paper it describes and who wrote the explanation.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The practice is moving toward more structured, reusable explanations tied to specific claims and model outputs. As research libraries grow, expect better linking between plain language summaries, extracted claims, and the underlying evidence. Automated drafting may assist, but human review will remain necessary to catch nuance and error. The likely direction is a tighter loop between publication, explanation, and post-publication critique.
